title: Comparing Gene-Level Selection on Coding Mutations Between Sample Groups Using Coselens
author: Iranzo, Gruenhagen, et al.

steps.title: Prepare mutation tables
steps.instruction: Create two separate mutation tables (one for the condition group and one for the control group). Each table must have exactly five columns in this order: sampleID, chr, pos, ref, alt. Include one row per observed mutation. Save the tables as R data frames or as text files (CSV or TSV). Ensure every listed mutation represents an independent event; if the same mutation appears in multiple related samples, keep only a single record and assign it arbitrarily to one sample. By default, coordinates must refer to the GRCh37/hg19 human reference; for other species or assemblies provide a RefCDS object via the refdb option.

steps.title: Filter ultrahypermutator samples
steps.instruction: Remove samples that are likely ultrahypermutators to avoid bias. Exclude any sample with more than 3,000 coding mutations per exome, or any sample whose total mutation count exceeds the mean by more than three standard deviations.

steps.title: Create optional input files
steps.instruction: Prepare additional files if needed: (a) a list of genes of interest (1‑column or 1‑row comma‑delimited, no header) to restrict results; (b) a list of sequenced genes (required only for targeted panels) in the same format; (c) an alternative reference database (RefCDS object) and, if desired, a covariate table for non‑human genomes or non‑GRCh37 assemblies. Use the dndscv buildref function or CrossMap to generate these objects.

steps.title: Identify candidate genes (optional)
steps.instruction: Run the dndscv R package on the combined mutation data to detect genes under significant positive selection. Use the resulting gene list as candidate genes for epistasis analysis.

steps.title: Split samples by candidate gene
steps.instruction: For each candidate gene, divide the full sample set into two groups: (1) samples that contain at least one coding mutation in the candidate gene, and (2) all remaining samples. If desired, apply stricter criteria (e.g., only truncating mutations for tumor‑suppressor genes or hotspot substitutions for oncogenes) to define the presence of a driver mutation.

steps.title: Run Coselens comparison
steps.instruction: Execute Coselens on the two groups for the current candidate gene. When appropriate, set the option subset.genes.by to the list of genes of interest to limit the Benjamini‑Hochberg correction to that subset.

steps.title: Filter significant results and format
steps.instruction: From the Coselens output object (coselens_out$substitutions), keep only rows with significant q‑values. Add a new leftmost column containing the name of the candidate gene. Remove the columns num.driver.group1, num.driver.group2, and dependency.

steps.title: Merge candidate results into network table
steps.instruction: Combine the filtered tables from all candidate genes into a single merged table. Each row now represents an edge of the epistasis network and must include the two gene names, the effect size (Delta.Nd), a qualitative interaction classification, and the associated p‑ and q‑values.

steps.title: Visualize and analyze epistasis network
steps.instruction: Load the merged table into Cytoscape (or use Python libraries such as NetworkX or igraph) to plot and explore the network. Optionally, run the SiMap tool on the table to detect network modules while accounting for the sign and weight of each link.

description: COnditional SELection on the Excess of NonSynonymous Substitutions (Coselens) is an R package to detect gene-level differential selection between two groups of samples. If the samples are grouped based on the value of a binary variable (e.g., the presence or absence of some environmental stress or phenotypic trait), Coselens identifies genes that harbor conditional driver mutations (that is, mutations whose adaptive value depends on the grouping variable). Coselens provides maximum likelihood estimates of the average number of driver mutations per gene per sample by comparing the observed number of coding (nonsynonymous and truncating) substitutions and indels with the number of mutations that would be expected in the absence of selection. Coselens also classifies instances of conditional selection based on their sign and the magnitude of their association with the independent variable. A major application of Coselens is to infer epistasis networks that can be later analyzed with appropriate tools to extract relevant biological information. The workflow to generate epistasis networks with Coselens is explained in the section quantification and statistical analysis. Coselens uses the dndscv R package2 to estimate a neutral mutation model that takes into account trinucleotide contexts and genomic covariates. As a result, Coselens is subject to the same assumptions as dndscv. Although explaining the use of dndscv is out of the scope of this protocol, we describe its critical assumptions in the data preparation and troubleshooting sections. Coselens also admits most of the optional parameters of dndscv. The most relevant of these parameters are described along the protocol. This section specifies the system requirements, installation instructions, and file formats required by Coselens.
